0-signer-authorization: The program accepts an account without verifying that it signed the transaction. Attackers can invoke privileged instructions using arbitrary accounts.
1-account-data-matching: The program trusts account data without validating that the supplied account belongs to the expected authority. Attackers may substitute accounts they do not own.
10-sysvar-address-checking: The program accepts a sysvar account without verifying its address. An attacker may provide a fake account that mimics the expected sysvar.
2-owner-checks: The program deserializes and trusts account data without verifying ownership. Malicious users can provide attacker-controlled accounts with forged data.
3-type-cosplay: Different account types can share compatible memory layouts. Without discriminator validation, an attacker can make one account type impersonate another.
4-initialization: The program allows account initialization without enforcing proper initialization checks, enabling account takeover or state corruption.
5-arbitrary-cpi: The program performs cross-program invocations without validating the target program. Attackers may redirect execution to malicious programs.
6-duplicate-mutable-accounts: The same mutable account may be supplied multiple times, causing unexpected state updates and logic manipulation.
7-bump-seed-canonicalization: Using non-canonical PDA bumps can allow attackers to generate alternative valid PDAs and bypass expected validation rules.
8-pda-sharing: A PDA reused across multiple trust domains can allow one workflow to interfere with another, leading to privilege escalation or data corruption.
9-closing-accounts: Improper account closure can leave reusable account state or permit account revival attacks after funds have been reclaimed.
